commonErrors.correction: Pressure statistics reward ineffective contact.| Count only actions that change possession, disposal or movement.

progressions: - Remove the breaks between scenario blocks.
- Allow captains to choose tactical adjustments.
- Increase match duration.
- Add opponent-specific patterns.
- Complete the rehearsal under controlled match fatigue.
regressions: - Use controlled contact rather than match-like tackling.
- Reduce player numbers and ground size.
- Allow coaches to organise each restart.
successIndicators: - Apply safe tackling at match speed.
- Adapt to tactical and scoreboard scenarios.
matchApplication: This rehearsal combines the chapter’s technical, tactical and decision-making content into one match environment. It prepares players for final assessment and identifies any remaining individual or team-pressure weaknesses.
relatedDrills: - TK-110 – Pressure Leadership and Tactical Assessment

title: Tackling and Pressure Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Final assessment of tackling and pressure capability
objective: Provide a complete chapter assessment of each player’s ability to execute safe tackles, make appropriate pressure decisions and contribute to coordinated team defence under match-like conditions.
groundSize: Full oval with six assessment zones and a final match-simulation area.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
- Construct six assessment zones:
- Zone 1: Fundamental tackle technique.
- Zone 2: Moving and evasive ball carriers.
- Zone 3: Disposal, ground-ball and contest decisions.
- Zone 4: Two- and three-player pressure.
- Zone 5: Tactical team-pressure systems.
- Zone 6: Match-scenario pressure and leadership.
- Finish with a full-ground match simulation.
- Assign qualified coaches or trained observers to every zone.
- Match players appropriately for size, maturity and contact capacity.
- Use controlled contact for developing players and match-like contact only for prepared senior players.
- Apply the same scoring system at every zone.
- Record individual technical, tactical, physical and communication outcomes.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. At Zone 1, players complete stationary, side-on and moving tackle entries.
2. Observers assess approach, head position, legal contact height, wrapping, control and release.
3. At Zone 2, defenders face live evasion, changes of pace, rear-quarter pursuit and fend-off situations.
4. Observers assess balance, patience, recovery and tackle timing.
5. At Zone 3, players select between tackle, corral and smother around disposal, ground-ball and aerial-contest situations.
6. Observers assess decision quality, opponent protection and free-kick discipline.
7. At Zone 4, defenders complete two-versus-two and three-player pressure activities.
8. Observers assess role allocation, receiver denial, communication and tackle support.
9. At Zone 5, teams complete stoppage, corridor, boundary and forward-half pressure scenarios.
10. Observers assess structure, pressure rotation and tactical execution.
11. At Zone 6, players manage scoreboard, fatigue, chaos and opposition tactical adjustments.
12. Observers assess leadership, match awareness and adaptability.
13. Each behaviour receives:
- 3 points: Consistently demonstrated independently at match standard.
- 2 points: Consistently demonstrated under controlled conditions.
- 1 point: Demonstrated inconsistently or after correction.
- 0 points: Not demonstrated or performed unsafely.
14. Any illegal, reckless or uncontrolled contact stops the repetition immediately.
15. Players complete a final match simulation in which chapter behaviours are observed without regular coach intervention.
16. Coaches produce an individual tackling-and-pressure development profile for every player.
coachingPoints: - Safety is the first and non-negotiable assessment standard.
- Contact must remain below the shoulders and above the knees.
- Head placement must remain beside or behind the opponent.
- No sling, lifting, rotation or unnecessary ground force is permitted.
- Players must decelerate before contact.
- Defenders should recognise when to tackle, corral, smother or delay.
- Vulnerable ground-ball and aerial-contest players must be protected.
- Tacklers must release promptly.
- Players must recover into the next defensive action.
- Team pressure requires one ball defender and connected support.
- Central and dangerous space should be protected.
- Communication and leadership must continue under fatigue.
- Match context should influence risk.
- Preventable free kicks reduce the assessment result.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Acceleration and deceleration into contact.
- Near-foot placement.
- Legal tackle height.
- Safe head position.
- Two-arm wrapping.
- Upright control and prompt release.
- Response to evasion, pace and fend-offs.
- Recovery after missed or broken tackles.
- Decision making around disposal.
- Protection of players over the football.
- Smother and corral selection.
- Receiver denial and defensive support.
- Pressure rotation after disposals.
- Corridor and boundary positioning.
- Stoppage and turnover reaction.
- Tactical adjustment.
- Communication and leadership.
- Technique under fatigue.
- Free-kick discipline.
- Transition after winning possession.

commonErrors.error: Player approaches contact without decelerating.| Restore the final short adjustment steps before reassessment.
commonErrors.correction: Head position moves in front of the ball carrier.| Return to side-on entry and reduce approach speed.

commonErrors.error: Tackler contacts high or below the knees.| Rebuild legal torso targeting under controlled conditions.
commonErrors.correction: Player reaches instead of completing a two-arm wrap.| Continue foot movement until close enough to secure the body.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts tackles from unsafe rear positions.| Reach the hip line and move beside the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Player tackles when corral or smother is required.| Reassess the possession and disposal cues before committing.

commonErrors.error: Tackler fails to release after a spill or whistle.| Make release behaviour part of every repetition.
commonErrors.correction: Player stops after the first pressure action.| Add recovery and next-action scoring.

commonErrors.error: Several defenders chase the ball carrier.| Allocate one pressure player and protect receivers with others.
commonErrors.correction: Team concedes central space while pressing.| Prioritise the corridor and greatest scoring threat.

commonErrors.error: Communication declines under fatigue.| Reduce work duration and require consistent role calls.
commonErrors.correction: Match urgency creates illegal contact.| Maintain technical standards regardless of score or time.

progressions: - Complete the assessment at full match intensity.
- Add opponent-specific tactical patterns.
- Use video review for individual tackle technique.
- Compare pressure KPIs with match data.
- Repeat selected zones under controlled fatigue.
- Allow player leaders to conduct the final review.
- Develop position-specific assessment standards.
- Reassess identified weaknesses after a targeted training block.
regressions: - Reduce contact from match-like to controlled.
- Use tackle bags before live opponents.
- Replace tackling with pressure touches where required.
- Reduce player numbers and field size.
- Return players to the relevant earlier chapter drills before reassessment.
successIndicators: - Use safe head and shoulder placement.
- Select tackle, corral, smother or delay appropriately.
- Adapt to tactical and match scenarios.
- Convert pressure into possession and controlled attack.
matchApplication: The final assessment determines whether players can transfer isolated tackling technique into safe, intelligent and coordinated match pressure. Successful players combine physical execution with decision making, communication, tactical awareness, discipline and repeat effort.
relatedDrills: - TK-060 – Pressure and Contest Block Assessment
- TK-080 – Team Pressure and Ball-Movement Assessment
- TK-110 – Pressure Leadership and Tactical Assessment
- TK-119 – Tackling and Pressure Match Rehearsal

title: Attacking Shape Foundations
primarySkill: Establishing an effective attacking shape around the football.
objective: Develop players’ understanding of how to form and maintain a balanced attacking shape that provides forward, lateral and release options for the player in possession.
groundSize: A rectangular area approximately 40 metres long by 30 metres wide, divided into three horizontal zones.
equipment: Three marker poles or cone gates
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic
setup:
Divide players into two attacking groups of equal size.
One group operates at a time while the other group observes or completes a separate ball-handling activity.
Place one starting player with the football at one end of the area.
Position three to five teammates ahead of the football across the width and depth of the area.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
No defenders are used initially.
Players must avoid standing in a straight horizontal or vertical line.
howTheDrillWorks:
The starting player begins with the football and scans the attacking shape ahead.
Teammates establish at least one forward option, one lateral option and one release option behind or beside the football.
The football is moved by kick or handball through the area while all players adjust their positions after every disposal.
The player who disposes must immediately move to create another support option rather than remaining stationary.
The group scores by carrying or disposing the football through the scoring gate without two attackers occupying the same running lane.
Players reset at the opposite end and repeat in the other direction.
After several repetitions, introduce a five-second limit for the player in possession.
Rotate the observing group into the activity.
coachingPoints: Create options in front of, beside and behind the player in possession.
Avoid forming a flat line across the ground.
Maintain enough separation for each player to remain a genuine disposal option.
Adjust immediately when the football changes position.
Communicate early using names, direction and available space.
The nearest player should provide quick support without crowding the ball carrier.
Players further from the football should maintain width and depth.
Continue moving after disposing of the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players establish multiple disposal angles before the ball carrier comes under pressure.
Whether players maintain width and depth rather than following the football.
Whether the disposer moves again after releasing the football.
Whether players communicate before the football arrives.
Whether the attacking shape adjusts as possession moves through each zone.
Whether players can identify when the shape has become too flat or congested.

commonErrors.error: All players move towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Hold wider players in their lanes and require one player to remain ahead of the football.

commonErrors.error: Players form a straight line across the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Stagger starting positions so each player is at a different depth.

commonErrors.error: The disposer stops after releasing the football.
commonErrors.correction: Require the disposer to run past, support behind or replace another player’s position.

commonErrors.error: Players call for the football after the ball carrier has already committed.
commonErrors.correction: Demand earlier communication and scanning before possession is received.

commonErrors.error: Support players stand too close together.
commonErrors.correction: Use cones to identify minimum spacing until players recognise the required distance.

progressions: Add one passive defender who applies shadow pressure to the player in possession.
Add a second defender who attempts to close the most obvious passing lane.
Require the group to use both sides of the area before scoring.
Introduce a turnover consequence if two attackers occupy the same lane.
Allow defenders to become fully active once the attacking shape is consistently maintained.
regressions: Use handball only over a smaller area.
Mark fixed starting positions for forward, lateral and release options.
Pause after each disposal and allow the coach to reposition players.
successIndicators: Provide at least three different disposal angles.
Move immediately after disposing of the football.
Reach the scoring gate without the shape collapsing around the ball carrier.
matchApplication: The drill introduces the basic attacking structure required whenever a team wins possession. Effective teams provide the ball carrier with options ahead of the football, across the ground and behind the contest. Maintaining this shape reduces congestion, improves possession retention and allows the team to move the football towards goal without relying on a single predictable option.
relatedDrills: DM-100 – Decision Making Chapter Final Assessment

title: Contact and Release Chain
primarySkill: Maintaining an attacking disposal chain through controlled contact.
objective: Teach players to remain composed through controlled contact and release possession to connected support without losing attacking momentum.
groundSize: A 35-metre-long by 20-metre-wide channel with three contact stations.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced
setup:
Mark three staggered contact stations through the channel.
Position one defender or pad holder at each station.
Divide attackers into groups of four.
Begin the football with the first attacker.
Position support runners behind and beside possession.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
Rotate contact roles regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first attacker carries towards the opening contact station.
The defender applies controlled body pressure.
The ball carrier protects possession and releases to a support runner.
The receiver continues towards the next contact station.
The previous disposer follows and becomes the next support option.
The sequence repeats through all three stations.
Support players must remain on different angles.
The group scores by reaching the final gate without a fumble or turnover.
Defenders may increase pressure gradually as technique improves.
Rotate all roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Lower the centre of gravity before contact.
Keep the football away from the defender.
Maintain balance through the contact.
Release before the tackle becomes complete.
Support players should remain visible.
The disposer must continue running.
Communicate the next support option early.
Avoid blind or backward handballs.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ball carrier braces safely.
Whether possession remains protected.
Whether support players maintain clear angles.
Whether the release occurs before control is lost.
Whether the disposer follows the football.
Whether technique remains composed under repeated contact.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier holds the football too long.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage earlier recognition and release.

commonErrors.error: Support runners move directly behind possession.
commonErrors.correction: Create angled support lanes.

commonErrors.error: The football is exposed to the defender.
commonErrors.correction: Carry on the protected side and use the body as a shield.

commonErrors.error: The disposer stops after contact.
commonErrors.correction: Require immediate follow-up running.

commonErrors.error: Players rush the handball before balance is established.
commonErrors.correction: Secure footing and control before release.

progressions: Replace pads with controlled live defenders.
Add a second defender at the final station.
Reduce the distance between stations.
Require players to choose between two support options.
Continue into a live scoring action.
successIndicators: Maintain execution across repeated contact efforts.
matchApplication: Attacking possession frequently continues through tackles, bumps and body pressure. Players must protect the football and release to support before the defence can create a stoppage or turnover.
relatedDrills: TK-120 – Tackling and Pressure Chapter Final Assessment
TO-013 – Numbers at the Contest Exit

title: Smother Recovery Connection
primarySkill: Recovering and reconnecting after an attacking disposal is smothered.
objective: Teach players to react immediately to a smothered kick or handball and create a connected second attacking possession.
groundSize: A 35-metre-long by 25-metre-wide area with a disposal zone and two recovery lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced
setup:
Position one ball carrier inside the disposal zone.
Position one defender close enough to pressure or smother.
Place two attacking support players in separate recovery lanes.
Position one additional defender beyond the zone.
Mark a scoring gate at the far end.
The initial defender alternates between allowing the disposal and attempting a controlled smother.
Rotate roles after each repetition.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier receives and prepares to dispose.
The defender applies immediate pressure and may attempt a controlled smother.
Support players remain active on separate angles.
If the disposal clears the defender, play continues towards the scoring gate.
If the football is smothered, the ball carrier and support players react immediately.
The nearest attacker attempts to recover the loose football.
Other attackers provide outside and rear support.
The second defender applies pressure to the recovery possession.
Attackers score two points for recovering the smother and reaching the gate.
Defenders score by winning the loose football and exiting through a side gate.
Reset after each outcome.
coachingPoints: Expect pressure on the disposal.
Support should remain active until the football clears the contest.
The original disposer must react immediately to the smother.
One player attacks the loose football while others spread.
Protect the recovery possession before releasing.
Avoid repeating the same blocked disposal line.
Use the recovery to change the attacking angle.
Apply pressure immediately if defenders win the loose football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether support players stop when the disposal begins.
Whether the original disposer reacts after the smother.
Whether one attacker takes responsibility for recovery.
Whether support forms on different angles.
Whether the next disposal avoids the original pressure line.
Whether defensive possession is pressured.

commonErrors.error: Players assume the disposal will clear the defender.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain active support until the football is safely released.

commonErrors.error: The original disposer stands still after the smother.
commonErrors.correction: Demand an immediate second effort.

commonErrors.error: Several attackers collide at the loose football.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate the nearest player to recover while others spread.

commonErrors.error: The recovery disposal follows the same blocked path.
commonErrors.correction: Change the angle through lateral or rear support.

commonErrors.error: Attackers stop if defenders recover first.
commonErrors.correction: Apply immediate pressure and prevent the exit.

progressions: Make the smother defender fully active.
Add another recovery defender.
Reduce the area.
Continue into a live scoring phase.
Add repeated smother and spoil scenarios.
regressions: Predetermine whether the disposal will be smothered.
matchApplication: Smothers create unpredictable loose footballs and rapid changes in advantage. Teams that react first and remain connected can recover the possession and continue attacking before defenders reorganise.

title: Centre-Bounce Scoring Chain
primarySkill: Converting centre-bounce possession into a coordinated scoring opportunity.
objective: Develop a complete attacking chain from centre-bounce possession through midfield exit, forward connection and scoring-method selection.
groundSize: Centre square to the attacking goal using full forward-half width.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert
setup:
Use realistic centre-bounce numbers.
Position rucks and midfielders inside the centre square.
Position wings outside the square.
Position forwards and defenders in normal attacking-half roles.
Use normal goals.
Begin every repetition with a centre bounce or controlled ball-up.
Assign one team as the primary attacking team for three repetitions before rotating.
Allow legal match-like contact appropriate to the playing group.
howTheDrillWorks:
Begin with a centre bounce.
Midfielders compete to win or receive the stoppage possession.
As possession is secured, attacking midfielders spread into forward, lateral and release lanes.
Wings adjust according to the exit side.
Forwards coordinate short, deep and clearing leads.
The ball carrier selects a direct entry, high-forward connection, handball surge or reset.
Play continues until a score, turnover or defensive exit.
Normal match scoring applies.
Award one bonus point for a clean centre-bounce exit.
Award another bonus point when the exit creates a controlled scoring opportunity.
If defenders win possession, they counterattack towards the opposite end gate.
Reset immediately for the next centre bounce.
Rotate ruck, midfield and forward roles after each block.
coachingPoints: Establish the intended exit before the bounce without becoming predictable.
Spread immediately after possession is won.
Wings must react to the actual exit rather than pre-empt it.
Forwards should coordinate movement with the midfield possession.
Protect the first possession before forcing an entry.
Use the high-forward connection when the direct route is covered.
Maintain support behind the ball carrier.
React immediately if the opposition wins the stoppage.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether midfielders create separate exit lanes.
Whether wings adjust to possession direction.
Whether forwards time their leads correctly.
Whether the ball carrier has multiple entry choices.
Whether the team maintains support behind possession.
Whether the attack creates a quality shot rather than a rushed entry.
Whether transition response is immediate after a lost stoppage.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders remain clustered after the stoppage win.
commonErrors.correction: Assign forward, lateral and release spread responsibilities.

commonErrors.error: Wings commit before possession direction is clear.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width and react to the actual exit.

commonErrors.error: Forwards lead before midfield control is established.
commonErrors.correction: Trigger movement when the first possession is secured.

commonErrors.error: The first ball carrier kicks blindly inside 50.
commonErrors.correction: Use the high-forward or release option when the direct entry is covered.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after a lost centre bounce.
commonErrors.correction: Make defensive transition part of the scoring system.

progressions: Change centre-bounce match-ups and structures.
Begin with the attacking team trailing late in the match.
Add a required scoring time limit.
Allow full-ground transition after turnovers.
Remove all coach communication during the repetition.
regressions: Pause after the stoppage win to organise spread.
matchApplication: Centre-bounce wins provide valuable scoring opportunities because both teams begin in structured positions. The advantage depends on clean exit, rapid spread and coordinated movement before the opposition can establish defensive support.
relatedDrills: RK-080 – Ruck and Stoppage Craft Chapter Final Assessment

title: Protect Lead and Counterattack
primarySkill: Protecting a late lead while remaining ready to counterattack.
objective: Teach players to retain possession and protect field position while recognising opportunities to counterattack and extend a late-game lead.
groundSize: Three-quarter ground or full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Set one team between one and twelve points ahead.
Set the clock between two and four minutes.
Begin the leading team in possession from varied field positions.
Use normal rules, boundaries and scoring.
Nominate time and field-position leaders.
The trailing team applies aggressive pressure.
Repeat with different leads and starting positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The leading team begins in possession.
Players assess whether to retain, advance, score or use the boundary.
The team maintains width and support behind possession.
If the opposition overcommits, attackers may launch a counterattack.
A counterattack should be taken only when the scoring chance is clear and turnover protection remains.
Turnovers are played live.
The scenario ends when time expires or the trailing team takes the lead.
Reset with a different score, time and field position.
Rotate leadership roles.
Coaches record risk decisions without interrupting play.
Review selected decisions.
Repeat the scenario under greater pressure.
coachingPoints: Know the score and remaining time.
Maintain active possession rather than standing still.
Use safe width, rear support and boundary positions.
Avoid unnecessary central turnovers.
Recognise when aggressive opposition pressure creates counterattacking space.
Counterattack with enough support to protect possession.
Take a clear score that extends the lead.
Maintain defensive balance behind every attacking action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether possession remains active and connected.
Whether players choose suitable field positions.
Whether the team becomes excessively defensive.
Whether counterattacking opportunities are recognised.
Whether enough players support the counterattack.
Whether defensive balance remains behind possession.
Whether scoreboard communication is accurate.

commonErrors.error: Players refuse every forward option.
commonErrors.correction: Take clear opportunities that extend the lead without excessive risk.

commonErrors.error: The team attacks centrally despite scoreboard control.
commonErrors.correction: Use safer width or boundary possession unless the central option is clearly open.

commonErrors.error: Players become stationary.
commonErrors.correction: Continue providing safe leads and replacement movement.

commonErrors.error: Too many players join the counterattack.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain defenders and rear support behind possession.

commonErrors.error: A counterattack begins without a genuine advantage.
commonErrors.correction: Retain possession until the defence overcommits.

progressions: Reduce the lead.
Increase opposition pressure.
Remove time reminders.
Begin from a defensive-half turnover.
Run repeated scenarios with limited recovery.
regressions: Give the leading team a numerical advantage.
Pause after turnovers to assess risk.
successIndicators: Preserve defensive balance until time expires.
matchApplication: Protecting a lead does not require abandoning attack. Effective teams control possession, manage field position and punish opposition overcommitment without exposing themselves to unnecessary turnover risk.
relatedDrills: TO-015 – Fast or Control Tempo Game

title: Rotating Match Scenario Circuit
primarySkill: Applying team offence across varied match scenarios.
objective: Prepare players to adapt their attacking method across a sequence of realistic match scenarios without losing the core principles of width, depth, connection and support.
groundSize: Full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Prepare scenario cards including:
Centre-bounce attack.
Kick-in to score.
Defensive turnover transition.
Boundary pressure escape.
Forward-half repeat entry.
Two-minute comeback.
Protecting a late lead.
Wet-weather possession.
Reduced-bench fatigue.
Attack against a changing defensive system.
Use normal match rules and scoring.
Assign line leaders and scoreboard communicators.
Rotate the starting scenario every four to six minutes.
Allow appropriate recovery and safety adjustment between high-load blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
Draw or select the first scenario.
Position players according to the match situation.
Begin live play.
The attacking team must identify the problem and select an appropriate method.
The defensive team applies realistic pressure and transitions after turnovers.
Normal scoring applies unless the scenario card provides a specific target.
Coaches assess attacking shape, decision quality, communication and outcome.
End the block when the scenario is completed or the nominated time expires.
Provide only brief feedback.
Select a different scenario.
Rotate leadership and specialist roles.
Complete the final two scenarios without coach feedback.
Finish with one unpredictable scenario selected during live play.
coachingPoints: Preserve width, depth and support in every scenario.
Identify the specific match problem quickly.
Select a method suited to score, time, field position and defence.
Communicate the plan across all three lines.
Adapt when the first option is removed.
Maintain possession quality under urgency.
Protect the team behind the football.
Apply immediate transition pressure after turnovers.
Retain core attacking principles when conditions change.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How quickly players understand each scenario.
Whether line leaders organise the team.
Whether the selected method suits the match problem.
Whether players adapt after the first option closes.
Whether scoreboard and time awareness influence decisions.
Whether attacking structure remains connected.
Whether transition response is immediate.
Whether performance standards survive repeated scenario changes.

commonErrors.error: Players use the previous scenario’s method in the new situation.
commonErrors.correction: Reassess score, time, field position and defensive structure before restarting.

commonErrors.error: Communication remains local.
commonErrors.correction: Use line leaders to relay the attacking plan across the ground.

commonErrors.error: Urgency causes loss of shape.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain width, depth and rear support while increasing decision speed.

commonErrors.error: Players become overly cautious after a turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish possession and attack the available opportunity.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue reduces tactical awareness.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the block and restore communication and positioning standards.

commonErrors.error: Core principles disappear when conditions change.
commonErrors.correction: Rebuild around connection, spacing and support before adding tactical detail.

progressions: Select scenarios without warning.
Change the defensive system during each block.
Reduce recovery between scenarios where safe.
Add numerical disadvantages.
Complete an extended final scenario under full match conditions.
regressions: Announce scenarios before players take position.
Provide the attacking team with a numerical advantage.
Pause midway through each scenario for correction.
successIndicators: Maintain width, depth and rear support.
Manage score, time and field position.
matchApplication: Teams must apply their attacking system in many different match situations. This circuit tests whether players can retain core offence principles while adapting tactics to score, time, field position, conditions and opposition structure.

title: Team Offence Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Applying the complete team-offence system under match conditions.
objective: Assess whether players can independently establish, maintain and adapt complete team offence from possession win through ball movement, forward entry, scoring and turnover response.
groundSize: Full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams using normal match positions.
Use full-ground dimensions and normal scoring.
Appoint defensive, midfield and forward leaders for both teams.
Prepare varied restarts and scenarios including:
Centre bounce.
Kick-in.
Defensive-half turnover.
Boundary pressure.
Forward-half repeat entry.
Late-game comeback.
Late-game lead protection.
Changing defensive system.
Wet-weather or difficult-ball simulation.
Reduced-rotation fatigue.
Assign coaches to assess separate components of team offence.
Use legal match-like contact appropriate to the playing group.
Provide no tactical coaching during the opening and final blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
Begin with a standard match restart.
Teams play under normal rules for an opening assessment block.
The team in possession must establish width, depth and support ahead, beside and behind the football.
Players select the appropriate route through the ground.
Forwards coordinate scoring threats and entry movement.
Turnovers are played live with immediate transition.
After the opening block, introduce selected match scenarios.
Each scenario continues until a score, turnover, stoppage outcome or time limit.
Normal match scoring applies.
Coaches also record assessment points for:
Establishing attacking shape.
Providing multiple disposal options.
Escaping pressure cleanly.
Advancing all three playing lines.
Using width, corridor, switch and reset appropriately.
Creating and using numerical advantages.
Selecting an effective forward-entry method.
Maintaining two-way scoring threats.
Adapting to defensive systems.
Managing score and time.
Protecting against turnover.
Communicating across all lines.
Provide concise feedback between middle blocks only.
Rotate line leaders and selected positional roles.
Complete a final eight-to-ten-minute block under normal match rules.
Do not provide coach intervention during the final block.
Complete the assessment record after play ends.
coachingPoints: Establish attacking shape immediately after gaining possession.
Maintain width without losing connection.
Provide options at different depths.
Preserve support behind the football.
Select tempo according to numbers, space and pressure.
Use switches and resets to move defensive structures.
Access the corridor only when reward justifies risk.
Coordinate midfield and forward movement.
Maintain aerial and ground-level support.
Adapt to changing defensive systems.
Manage score, time and field position.
Communicate the attacking method across all three lines.
Protect the team against turnover.
Maintain standards under fatigue and match-like pressure.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether attacking shape forms without coach direction.
Whether the ball carrier consistently receives several options.
Whether width, depth and rear support remain connected.
Whether players away from the football maintain useful structure.
Whether pressure possessions are released cleanly.
Whether all three playing lines advance together.
Whether switches and resets create improved attacking pictures.
Whether corridor decisions are appropriately balanced.
Whether numerical advantages are identified and used.
Whether forwards coordinate short, deep, clearing and weak-side movement.
Whether scoring-method selection suits the defensive structure.
Whether players adapt to zone, press and man-on-man systems.
Whether scoreboard and time affect risk selection.
Whether leaders organise the team effectively.
Whether turnover protection and transition response are immediate.
Whether execution and decision quality survive fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Players crowd possession after winning the football.
commonErrors.correction: Restore forward, lateral, wide and rear support roles.

commonErrors.error: The team becomes flat across the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish staggered depth between playing lines.

commonErrors.error: Weak-side players follow the football.
commonErrors.correction: Hold useful width and remain a genuine attacking threat.

commonErrors.error: Ball movement does not alter the defence.
commonErrors.correction: Change angle, tempo, depth or side with purpose.

commonErrors.error: Players force corridor possession.
commonErrors.correction: Assess receiver separation, next options and turnover consequence.

commonErrors.error: Switches finish with an isolated receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Move all three lines and provide forward, inside and rear support.

commonErrors.error: Forward entries become predictable.
commonErrors.correction: Use varied leading, running, contest and possession methods.

commonErrors.error: Numerical advantages become congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the free player outside defensive pressure.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to adapt to defensive changes.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate the new system and select a collective response.

commonErrors.error: Scoreboard urgency causes reckless disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Increase decision speed without abandoning execution quality.

commonErrors.error: The team becomes passive while protecting a lead.
commonErrors.correction: Retain active possession and attack clear opportunities.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes loss of structure.
commonErrors.correction: Rotate roles and return to core spacing and connection principles.

commonErrors.error: Turnovers expose the team behind the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain defensive balance and immediate transition response.

progressions: Remove all scenario warnings and coach prompts.
Change defensive systems during open play.
Add score, time, field-position and numerical-disadvantage conditions.
Increase match-like contact where appropriate.
Complete an extended full-match simulation.
Use the assessment results to assign individual and line-specific development priorities.
regressions: Assess one phase of team offence at a time.
Provide the attacking team with a numerical advantage.
Pause between phases for structural feedback.
Shorten work blocks for younger, returning or masters players.
successIndicators: Maintain width, depth and rear support.
Advance defensive, midfield and forward lines together.
Use wing, corridor, switch, reset and overload options appropriately.
Coordinate forward movement and scoring threats.
Maintain decision quality and execution under fatigue.
Apply the complete team-offence system without constant coach direction.
matchApplication: This final assessment combines the complete Team Offence chapter from TO-001 to TO-099. It determines whether players can convert possession into organised, adaptable and efficient attack across technical, tactical, pressure, positional and match-scenario demands.
relatedDrills: TO-040 – Team Offence Running Patterns Assessment
TO-060 – Pressure and Contest Mastery Assessment
TO-080 – Team Ball Movement Final Assessment

title: Turnover Recognition Reset
primarySkill: Recognising a change of possession.
objective: Develop players’ ability to immediately recognise whether their team has gained or lost possession and adopt the correct attacking or defensive position without waiting for further instruction.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 25 metres wide, divided into one central possession area and four outside positioning gates.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a central 20-metre × 20-metre possession area.
Place two wide attacking gates outside the left and right edges of the area.
Place two narrow defensive gates closer to the corridor.
Divide players into two evenly numbered teams.
One team begins with the football while the other team shadows without applying contact.
The coach stands outside the area with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession moves the football by kick or handball inside the central area.
Players without possession maintain light shadow pressure but cannot intercept initially.
The coach calls “turnover” and either gives the football to the other team or rolls a new football into the area.
Players must immediately call either “ours” or “theirs” according to the new possession state.
The team gaining possession spreads towards the two wide attacking gates.
The team losing possession compresses towards the two central defensive gates.
Players hold their new structure for three seconds before play resumes.
After several repetitions, allow defenders to intercept naturally so the turnover cue becomes less predictable.
Rotate the starting team after each one-minute block.
coachingPoints: Players must identify possession change before beginning their movement.
Encourage loud, early communication from more than one player.
The team gaining possession should create width and depth rather than crowding the football.
The team losing possession should protect the corridor before chasing outside.
Players nearest the football should respond differently from players positioned further away.
Avoid all players reacting directly towards the football.
Players should scan before the turnover so their first movement is informed.
Reinforce immediate role change without disappointment, hesitation or argument.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players recognise the change of possession immediately.
Whether communication occurs before movement.
Whether attacking players create usable width and depth.
Whether defensive players compress towards dangerous central space.
Whether players continue performing their previous role after possession changes.
Whether the nearest players and furthest players adopt appropriate different responses.

commonErrors.error: Players continue moving as though their team still has possession.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the repetition and require players to call “ours” or “theirs” before moving.

commonErrors.error: Every player runs directly towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign outside players responsibility for width and inside players responsibility for corridor protection.

commonErrors.error: Players react only after the coach gives a second instruction.
commonErrors.correction: Remove the second instruction and reward the first team that reorganises independently.

commonErrors.error: Communication comes after the movement has already started.
commonErrors.correction: Require the possession call to be made immediately when the football changes teams.

commonErrors.error: Players walk into their transition positions.
commonErrors.correction: Set a three-second movement target while keeping the drill non-contact.

progressions: Allow defenders to intercept passes naturally rather than relying on the coach’s turnover call.
Add a three-second scoring bonus when the attacking team reaches a wide gate quickly.
Add a central scoring gate that the defending team must protect.
Increase the number of players and enlarge the area.
Allow full live play for 15-second periods after each turnover.
regressions: Use only four players per team.
Walk players through the attacking and defensive shapes before beginning.
Use a whistle and clear visual signal for each possession change.
Remove the football and practise the movements as a recognition exercise.
Give each player a fixed attacking and defensive starting position.
successIndicators: Change direction within one second of the turnover.
Protect central space before chasing wide.
Perform the transition response without waiting for the coach.
matchApplication: Australian football regularly changes from attack to defence or defence to attack without a stoppage. Players who recognise the turnover quickly can create an immediate numerical advantage, close dangerous space, provide an outlet or prevent the opposition from using the corridor.

title: Attack-to-Defence Recovery
primarySkill: Recovering defensively after losing possession in attack.
objective: Develop the ability to recover from an attacking position into an organised defensive shape immediately after possession is lost.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide with an attacking scoring zone, a central recovery line and a counterattack scoring gate.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark an attacking scoring zone at one end of the area.
Mark a counterattack gate at the opposite end.
Place a recovery line approximately 15 metres behind the attacking scoring zone.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Begin with the attacking team positioned ahead of the recovery line.
Position the defending team compactly near the scoring zone.
The coach stands near the attacking end with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession and attempts to enter the scoring zone.
The defending team applies controlled pressure and attempts to intercept or win the football.
When the defending team gains possession, it immediately counterattacks towards the opposite scoring gate.
The player nearest the turnover applies pressure to delay the counterattack.
Other former attacking players sprint goal-side and recover through or towards the central recovery line.
Recovering players must protect the corridor before defending wider options.
The counterattacking team scores two points for reaching the opposite gate and one point for carrying or disposing through the recovery line.
The recovering team scores one point for forcing the football wide and two points for regaining possession before the opposition reaches the gate.
Reset after a score, turnover, boundary exit or 30 seconds of play.
Swap attacking and defending roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: The nearest player should pressure and delay rather than attempting an unrealistic immediate tackle.
Players further from the football must recover goal-side at speed.
Recovery runs should be directed towards dangerous space, not simply towards an opponent.
Protect the corridor before defending lower-risk boundary space.
Players should communicate who is pressuring, covering and protecting the deepest option.
Defenders must avoid running past the ball carrier and opening a central lane.
Once the counterattack is slowed, the defensive group should balance and match opponents.
Transition running should continue until the defence is organised, not only until players cross the recovery line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the nearest player delays the counterattack.
The direction and speed of recovery runs.
Whether players protect central space.
Whether recovering players identify the most dangerous opponent.
Whether communication establishes clear defensive roles.
Whether players stop running once they reach the recovery line.
Whether the team can convert frantic recovery into an organised defensive shape.

commonErrors.error: Players chase the football from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Direct off-ball players to recover goal-side and protect the corridor.

commonErrors.error: The nearest player dives in and is evaded.
commonErrors.correction: Coach the player to close space under control and delay the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Recovering players run towards wide opponents first.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise central space and the deepest dangerous option.

commonErrors.error: Players jog after losing possession.
commonErrors.correction: Score transition effort and rotate players who repeatedly fail to recover.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recover to the same line with no depth.
commonErrors.correction: Establish pressure, cover and deeper balance roles.

progressions: Introduce full tackling.
Add an extra counterattacking player to create numerical disadvantage.
Begin the attacking team deeper inside the scoring zone.
Allow the counterattacking team only eight seconds to score.
Require the recovering team to win possession and immediately counterattack back.
Increase the field width to create more difficult defensive decisions.
regressions: Give the recovering team a numerical advantage.
Require the counterattacking team to complete one sideways disposal before advancing.
Use touch pressure rather than tackling.
Reduce the required recovery distance for Over 35 players or returning players.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor before wide space.
Communicate dangerous opponents and open space.
Prevent direct, uncontested counterattack through the centre.
matchApplication: When a team turns the football over during an attacking phase, many players may be positioned ahead of the ball. Effective attack-to-defence transition requires immediate pressure and purposeful recovery to prevent the opposition from counterattacking through an exposed corridor.

title: Defence-to-Attack Spread
primarySkill: Spreading into attacking positions after regaining possession.
objective: Develop an immediate and coordinated attacking spread after a defensive regain so the ball carrier has safe, progressive and clearly separated disposal options.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 35 metres wide with four outlet gates positioned outside a compact defensive zone.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a compact 20-metre × 20-metre defensive zone in the centre of the area.
Position two wide outlet gates on each side of the area.
Position one forward gate and one deeper safety gate.
Divide players into a defending team and an attacking pressure team.
The defending team begins compactly inside the central zone.
The pressure team begins around the outside and sends the football into the zone.
The coach stands outside the area with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The pressure team kicks or handballs the football into the central defensive zone.
The defending team attempts to intercept, mark, spoil to advantage or win the ground ball.
Once possession is secured, the defending team immediately becomes the attacking team.
The first player outside the contest provides width on the nearest side.
A second player creates an option on the opposite side.
One player pushes forward while another remains behind the football as a safety option.
The team must exit through one of the four outlet gates while retaining possession.
Two points are awarded for using a forward or opposite-side outlet and one point for using the nearest safe outlet.
The opposition applies controlled pressure and attempts to lock the football inside the central zone.
Reset when the football exits through a gate, is turned over or leaves the playing area.
coachingPoints: The first attacking movement should create separation from the contest.
Players should spread to different lanes rather than following the same path.
The player winning possession must be supported from the front, side and behind.
Width should be created before the opposition can establish a press.
The ball carrier should use the safest progressive option, not automatically the nearest teammate.
Opposite-side players must remain engaged and available for a switch.
Players should avoid all running forward and leaving no support behind the football.
Communication should identify wide, forward and safety options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How quickly players leave the compact defensive shape.
Whether players create width on both sides.
Whether forward and safety options are available.
Whether players crowd the first possession.
Whether the ball carrier scans the full field.
Whether the team selects a safe but progressive exit.
Whether the opposite side remains available for a switch.

commonErrors.error: Players remain in a defensive cluster after winning possession.
commonErrors.correction: Use outlet gates to give each player a clear spreading responsibility.

commonErrors.error: All players run forward.
commonErrors.correction: Require one designated safety player to remain behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Players spread to the same side.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate near-side, far-side, forward and rear support roles.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier uses the closest option without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require a visible head turn before disposal.

commonErrors.error: Wide players move too early and become disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Time the spread to occur as possession is being secured.

progressions: Allow full pressure after possession is won.
Add a second disposal requirement before the team can exit.
Award extra points for switching to the opposite side.
Reduce the width of the outlet gates.
Add a recovering defender outside the central zone.
Continue play into a second attacking phase after the exit.
regressions: Remove opposition pressure after the regain.
Nominate the required exit before the repetition.
Allow the coach to pause play and reposition players.
Use handball only for younger players.
successIndicators: Spread within two seconds of the regain.
Create width on both sides of the contest.
Exit without crowding the ball carrier.
Retain possession through the first exit.
matchApplication: After an intercept mark, spoil recovery or ground-ball win in defence, players must quickly expand from a compact defensive shape into an attacking shape. Effective spread creates exit options before the opposition can establish repeat pressure.

title: Boundary Contest Rebound
primarySkill: Rebounding from a contested possession near the boundary.
objective: Develop the ability to secure a boundary-side contest and transition into open space without forcing a high-risk central disposal.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 30 metres wide with a narrow boundary contest lane and two exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a five-metre-wide contest lane along one boundary.
Place a safe boundary exit gate ahead of the contest.
Place a higher-value central release gate on the opposite side of the area.
Divide players into two teams.
Position three to five players from each team near the contest lane.
Position outside support players through the central and far-side space.
The coach begins each repetition with a ground ball, high ball or pressured pass into the boundary lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both teams contest for the football inside the boundary lane.
The team gaining possession must establish control before selecting an exit.
A nearby teammate provides a safe down-the-line option.
Central and far-side players provide release options away from the boundary.
The boundary gate scores one point.
The central release gate scores three points but may only be used when the receiver has clear separation.
A central turnover gives the opposition three points.
The team losing possession applies immediate pressure and attempts to trap the football near the boundary.
Play continues until an exit, turnover, stoppage or 30-second limit.
Alternate the starting boundary after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Secure possession before attempting to move away from the boundary.
The safe down-the-line option should remain available.
Central release should be used only when the lane is genuinely clear.
Support players must not all enter the boundary congestion.
The ball winner should protect the football from boundary-side pressure.
Players behind the football should provide a reset.
The defending team should use the boundary as an extra defender.
Far-side players must remain engaged as potential switch options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Body positioning near the boundary.
Whether the ball winner protects possession.
Whether safe and aggressive exits are both available.
Whether players force central disposals.
Whether outside support stays separated.
Whether defenders trap the football against the boundary.
Whether the team can later access central space after securing possession.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt an immediate blind disposal into the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the football and confirm the central receiver is clear.

commonErrors.error: All teammates crowd the boundary contest.
commonErrors.correction: Keep outside players in release positions.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier steps over the boundary unnecessarily.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the football while maintaining awareness of the line.

commonErrors.error: Players ignore the safe down-the-line option.
commonErrors.correction: Retain a boundary outlet when the centre is closed.

commonErrors.error: Defenders allow an easy inside release.
commonErrors.correction: Pressure from the corridor side and force play towards the line.

progressions: Reduce the contest-lane width.
Add full controlled tackling.
Remove the marked exit gates.
Require a switch after a successful boundary exit.
Add a recovering defender in central space.
Continue into a full-ground transition phase.
regressions: Give the ball-winning team an extra outside player.
Stop briefly after possession is secured.
Reduce contact for younger or returning players.
successIndicators: Secure contested possession near the boundary.
Use central space only when clearly available.
Escape the boundary pressure with retained possession.
matchApplication: Boundary contests reduce space and often attract numbers. Teams must secure the football, maintain a safe outlet and recognise when central space is genuinely available rather than forcing a dangerous release.

title: Corridor Break and Hold Width
primarySkill: Breaking through the corridor while preserving outside width.
objective: Develop a central transition that attacks through the corridor without drawing every supporting player into the same lane.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 55 metres wide with a central corridor and two outside support lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central corridor approximately 15 metres wide.
Mark one outside support lane on each side.
Place a scoring gate at the attacking end.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Begin the transitioning team with possession near the defensive end.
Position defenders to pressure the corridor progressively.
Require at least one attacking player to remain in each outside lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
The transitioning team attempts to move possession through the corridor.
Central receivers lead into space and release before pressure closes.
Outside players hold width and remain available for release.
If the corridor remains open, the team may continue directly.
If defenders collapse centrally, the football is released to an outside lane.
One point is awarded for each controlled corridor possession.
Two points are awarded for breaking beyond the midfield line.
A bonus point is awarded when both outside lanes remain occupied.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching the scoring gate.
Defenders receive three points for forcing a central turnover.
Roles reverse immediately after a turnover.
Reset after a score, turnover or 40 seconds.
coachingPoints: Corridor players should receive while moving.
Outside players must resist following the football centrally.
The ball carrier should scan wide before central pressure arrives.
Width provides an escape and stretches the defence.
Support should remain behind as well as ahead of possession.
Central disposals must lead receivers away from pressure.
The team should avoid forcing corridor play when numbers close.
Players must transition defensively after a central turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Timing of corridor leads.
Whether outside width is maintained.
Whether central receivers scan before possession.
Quality of disposals through the corridor.
Whether players recognise collapsing pressure.
Whether safety support remains behind the football.
Defensive reaction after a central turnover.

commonErrors.error: Every player follows the football into the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one option in each outside lane.

commonErrors.error: Central receivers stand still.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into the corridor as the previous player prepares to dispose.

commonErrors.error: The team forces the next central possession.
commonErrors.correction: Release wide when the corridor compresses.

commonErrors.error: Wide players become too disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust width so they remain within achievable disposal distance.

commonErrors.error: No player protects behind the central chain.
commonErrors.correction: Retain a trailing security player.

progressions: Remove the lane markers.
Add full match-like pressure.
Reduce the corridor width.
Add a recovering defender from behind.
Continue into a live forward entry.
Introduce scoreboard conditions that alter risk.
regressions: Reduce repeat running for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Release to outside space when required.
Prevent central turnovers from becoming direct scores.
matchApplication: Corridor transition can move the football quickly towards goal, but it becomes dangerous when every player compresses centrally. Maintaining outside width protects possession and preserves alternative routes.

title: False Corridor Entry
primarySkill: Using apparent corridor movement to create outside transition space.
objective: Develop coordinated movement that presents a credible corridor threat before releasing possession into outside space created by defensive compression.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 55 metres wide with a central corridor and two wide scoring lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central corridor approximately 15 metres wide.
Mark a wide scoring lane on each side.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Position two central attacking receivers and wide players on both sides.
Begin with a defensive or midfield regain.
Position defenders to react strongly to central leads.
Retain at least one safety player behind the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The transitioning team secures possession.
One or two central players lead visibly into the corridor.
The ball carrier presents as though the next disposal will travel centrally.
Defenders compress towards the corridor leads.
Wide players hold their lanes and prepare to receive.
The ball carrier releases to the side offering the greatest space.
One point is awarded when central movement draws defenders.
Two points are awarded for completing the wide release.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching a wide scoring gate.
Defenders receive three points for holding width and intercepting the release.
Roles reverse after a turnover.
Reset after a score, turnover or 40 seconds.
coachingPoints: The corridor movement must be credible enough to influence defenders.
Central players should not obstruct each other or become stationary targets.
Wide players must maintain width and timing.
The ball carrier should scan both sides before presenting centrally.
Release timing is critical once defenders compress.
Safety support must remain behind the initial movement.
The corridor may still be used when defenders fail to compress.
Players must avoid turning the pattern into a predetermined fake.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the central leads appear genuine.
Whether defenders compress.
Whether wide players maintain separation.
Timing and direction of the release.
Whether the ball carrier scans both sides.
Whether the team uses the corridor when it remains available.
Whether defensive balance remains behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Central players make token movements that do not influence defenders.
commonErrors.correction: Lead with speed and present as genuine receiving options.

commonErrors.error: Wide players drift in before the release.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the defence commits centrally.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier decides the release side before scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Assess both wide lanes after defenders move.

commonErrors.error: The team refuses an open corridor because the drill expects width.
commonErrors.correction: Use the central option when defenders do not close it.

commonErrors.error: Security players follow the central leads.
commonErrors.correction: Remain connected behind possession.

progressions: Remove the corridor and lane markers.
Add full match-like pressure.
Allow defenders to disguise whether they will compress.
Introduce a second wide release after the first is closed.
Continue into a forward-entry phase.
Add scoreboard and time pressure.
regressions: Give the transitioning team a numerical advantage.
Reduce the number of central receivers.
successIndicators: Retain the corridor when it remains open.
matchApplication: Teams can create outside transition space by presenting a genuine central threat. Defenders who compress towards the corridor may leave wide lanes available for fast release.
relatedDrills: TR-072 – Corridor Break and Hold Width

title: Floating Player Transition Rotation
primarySkill: Integrating a floating player without losing team balance.
objective: Develop coordinated use of a floating transition player while ensuring teammates rotate to maintain width, line connection and defensive security.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 50 metres wide with defensive, midfield and attacking thirds.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the field into defensive, midfield and attacking thirds.
Divide players into two teams.
Add one neutral floating player who supports the team in possession.
The floating player may move anywhere.
Begin each phase with a defensive or midfield regain.
Require teams to maintain at least two players behind the football.
Rotate the floating role every three minutes.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team gains possession and may use the floating player.
The floating player moves to become the most useful transition connection.
A teammate must rotate to preserve team width or security when the float moves.
The team receives one point for using the float to complete a line-breaking possession.
One point is awarded for a successful role rotation around the float.
Two points are awarded for entering the attacking third.
Two additional points are awarded for scoring.
If the football turns over, the float immediately supports the new attacking team.
Both teams must reorganise around the float’s new position.
A turnover caused by losing behind-ball security gives the opposition a bonus point.
Play in three-minute blocks.
Rotate the float and restart from varied locations.
coachingPoints: The floating player should move to solve the current transition problem.
Teammates must not simply follow the float.
When the float moves forward, another player may need to replace behind.
When the float moves wide, central connection must remain.
The float should communicate the role being provided.
Players must reorganise immediately after a turnover.
The team should avoid overusing the neutral player when direct options exist.
The float must receive in space with a clear next action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the float moves to a useful location.
Whether teammates rotate around the movement.
Whether width and security are preserved.
Whether the team overuses the floating player.
Whether the float has a next option.
Whether teams reorganise after turnovers.
Whether the float communicates the role being provided.

commonErrors.error: Teammates crowd around the floating player.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain normal spacing and use the float as one option.

commonErrors.error: The float runs ahead and leaves no security.
commonErrors.correction: Require a teammate to replace behind before the movement continues.

commonErrors.error: Players automatically dispose to the neutral player.
commonErrors.correction: Use direct team options when they provide greater advantage.

commonErrors.error: The float receives without a next action.
commonErrors.correction: Move into positions that connect at least two teammates or lines.

commonErrors.error: Teams react slowly when the float changes sides after turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Reorganise immediately around the new possession team.

progressions: Add a second floating player with different movement restrictions.
Limit the number of float possessions.
Add full match-like pressure.
Remove the marked thirds.
Introduce scoreboard and time conditions.
Allow the defending team to temporarily deny the float.
regressions: Restrict the float to the midfield third.
Stop after turnovers to review rotations.
Keep three players behind the football.
Use shorter blocks for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Use the float to connect lines or break pressure.
matchApplication: Some players naturally become transition connectors by moving across positional lines. The team must use their movement without abandoning width, role balance or protection behind the football.

title: Midfield Unit Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing position-specific midfield transition responsibilities.
objective: Develop coordinated transition roles for inside midfielders, outside midfielders and defensive midfield support during repeated possession changes.
groundSize: Central 80 metres of the ground, including the centre square and both half-back and half-forward areas.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central playing area extending from half-back to half-forward.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two midfield units.
Within each unit, identify:
Inside ball winner
Defensive midfielder
Forward-running midfielder
Outside midfielder
Underneath support midfielder
Begin from stoppages, loose footballs and coach-created turnovers.
Rotate roles every four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins with a midfield contest or controlled possession.
When a team gains possession, the inside ball winner secures and releases the football.
The outside midfielder provides width.
The forward-running midfielder moves ahead into attacking connection.
The underneath midfielder supports behind the football.
When possession is lost, the nearest midfielder pressures.
The defensive midfielder protects the corridor and tracks the most dangerous runner.
Other midfielders recover goal-side and reconnect with defenders.
The attacking team receives one point for exiting the contest and two points for reaching its scoring gate.
The defending team receives one point for forcing a backwards disposal and three for regaining possession.
Play continues through repeated turnovers for up to 45 seconds.
Reset and review role execution after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Inside midfielders must secure possession before releasing.
Outside midfielders should preserve width rather than entering every contest.
One midfielder should support underneath the football.
Forward runners must time movement to possession security.
The nearest player pressures after a turnover.
Defensive midfielders protect the corridor and dangerous runners.
Midfielders must work in both directions rather than specialising in one phase.
Communication should identify inside, outside, hold, recover and deepest roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether midfielders maintain role diversity.
Security of the first possession.
Outside width during the transition.
Timing of forward-running midfielders.
Availability of underneath support.
Corridor protection after turnovers.
Defensive tracking effort.
Whether role clarity remains under fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Every midfielder attacks the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold one outside player and one underneath support player.

commonErrors.error: Forward runners leave before possession is secure.
commonErrors.correction: Time the run to the ball winner’s control.

commonErrors.error: No midfielder supports behind the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign an underneath connection and security role.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders chase direct opponents into wide space.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor and most dangerous runner first.

commonErrors.error: Players perform only attacking or defensive work.
commonErrors.correction: Rotate roles and score two-way transition actions.

progressions: Remove marked midfield roles.
Add full match-like stoppage contact.
Introduce changing numerical balance.
Continue from midfield into full forward entries.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require role handovers during the same phase.
regressions: Give the possession team a neutral midfielder.
Shorten repeated running for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: Midfielders are central to transition because they influence both the initial contest and the connection between defence and attack. Effective midfield units maintain role balance rather than sending every player towards the same action.

title: Wing Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing wing-specific attacking and defensive transition roles.
objective: Develop wing players’ ability to provide attacking width, switch connection and defensive corridor support according to ball location and possession state.
groundSize: Approximately 80 metres long × 60 metres wide, using both wings and the corridor.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a near-side wing, corridor and far-side wing.
Place one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Assign one wing player to each side for both teams.
Position other players through half-back, midfield and half-forward.
Begin from defensive and midfield regains on alternating sides.
Rotate wing players every four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team gains possession near a boundary or through the corridor.
The near-side wing provides an immediate outside or forward option.
The far-side wing holds width and prepares for a switch.
If the team loses possession, the near-side wing pressures or tracks the outside outlet.
The far-side wing folds towards the corridor while preserving far-side awareness.
When possession changes again, both wings expand quickly.
One point is awarded for effective near-side support.
One point is awarded for maintaining usable far-side width.
Two points are awarded for a successful switch through a wing.
The defending team receives two points when a wing’s recovery closes a dangerous lane.
Play continues through repeated turnovers for 40 seconds.
Reset and alternate the starting side.
coachingPoints: Near-side and far-side wing roles differ.
The near-side wing should support the immediate possession phase.
The far-side wing must maintain width without becoming disconnected.
After losing possession, wings should fold enough to protect the corridor.
Wings must scan inside and behind, not only follow the boundary.
Far-side width can become the best attacking option after a regain.
Wing players should preserve the ability to move in both directions.
Communication should identify switch, fold, hold and inside support.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Position of near-side and far-side wings.
Whether far-side width remains usable.
Whether wings fold appropriately in defence.
Timing of switch movement.
Whether wing receivers have inside support.
Whether players become trapped against the boundary.
Two-way running effort.
Role adjustment after repeated turnovers.

commonErrors.error: Both wings move to the same side of the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve far-side width and team balance.

commonErrors.error: The far-side wing remains too wide after possession is lost.
commonErrors.correction: Fold towards the corridor while tracking the switch threat.

commonErrors.error: The near-side wing stands flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into space and provide a moving outlet.

commonErrors.error: Wings receive without inside support.
commonErrors.correction: Connect a midfielder or half-back beneath the wing.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after a switch disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue supporting the next forward action.

progressions: Remove wing-lane markers.
Add full match-like pressure.
Require wing players to rotate with half-backs and half-forwards.
Continue into a full forward-entry phase.
Introduce hidden switch traps.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
regressions: Stop after each turnover to review wing positioning.
Reduce repeated running for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Execute different near-side and far-side roles.
matchApplication: Wing players provide critical balance during transition. Their positioning determines whether the team can access width in attack while still protecting the corridor and opposite-side movement in defence.
relatedDrills: TR-063 – Wing Release and Inside Support

title: Forward Unit Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing forward-specific transition roles after gaining or losing possession.
objective: Develop clear transition roles for deep forwards, high forwards and pressure forwards during forward entries, defensive exits and forward-half regains.
groundSize: Forward half of an oval, including forward 50 and high half-forward space.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use one forward half.
Divide players into a forward unit and defensive unit.
Within the forward unit, identify:
Deep forward
High forward
Pressure forwards
Forward-half security player
Mark near-side, corridor and far-side defensive exits.
Begin each repetition with a forward entry.
Vary whether the entry is marked, spoiled, intercepted or won at ground level.
howTheDrillWorks:
The forward unit organises leads and support during the entry.
If the forward team wins possession, it attempts to create a controlled scoring opportunity.
If the defensive team regains possession, forward roles immediately change.
The nearest pressure forward closes the ball carrier.
Other pressure forwards deny the short and corridor exits.
The high forward protects the next release or midfield connection.
The deep forward either pressures locally or protects the dangerous switch route according to position.
If the forward team regains possession, players spread into direct, wide and underneath scoring options.
The forward unit receives three points for a goal and two points for a repeat entry.
The defensive unit receives three points for a controlled exit.
Play continues for up to 40 seconds.
Reset and rotate forward roles.
coachingPoints: Forward transition begins immediately when an entry is lost.
The nearest forward pressures while others close exits.
High forwards must protect the connection beyond defensive 50.
Deep forwards should avoid chasing harmless possession away from goal.
Forward-half regains should be secured before a rushed shot.
Players must create varied scoring options after regaining possession.
At least one player should remain behind the attacking contest.
Communication should identify pressure, corridor, switch and deepest roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Reaction after a lost forward entry.
Nearest-player pressure.
Coverage of corridor and short exits.
High-forward positioning.
Whether deep forwards chase unnecessarily.
Quality of forward-half regains.
Organisation of scoring options.
Security behind the attacking contest.

commonErrors.error: Every forward chases the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Assign pressure, outlet-denial and deeper-cover roles.

commonErrors.error: The high forward moves too deep into the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold position to protect the next defensive exit.

commonErrors.error: Deep forwards stop after an intercepted entry.
commonErrors.correction: Pressure locally or protect the dangerous route.
